intro: Rachmaninoff plays his own piano version of Lilacs, a song about a search for happiness among flowers. The melody nestles inside the right hand’s rippling notes, with little cadenzas growing around it.

sections.label: A · A song inside the triplets
sections.mNote: Non allegro; the right hand carries tune and accompaniment

sections.label: B · A trill holds the music still
sections.mNote: Accelerando and crescendo lead to a fermata

sections.label: C · High notes and the final run
sections.mNote: The tune passes between hands before a veloce flourish

cues.title: A song inside the hand
cues.text: Two quiet bars of triplets, then the melody enters beneath them. The right hand plays both at once: its thumb carries the song while the upper fingers keep moving. The left hand joins with widely spaced broken chords in A♭ major.
cues.evidence: Piano transcription, Piano Street scan, p. 1: Non allegro, opening triplets, melody in the lower right-hand voice and left-hand arpeggios. https://www.pianostreet.com/rachmaninoff-sheet-music/transcriptions/lilacs.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Beketova’s lilacs
cues.text: In 1902 Rachmaninoff sets Ekaterina Beketova’s poem about lilacs and the search for happiness. Eleven years later he brings the song back to the piano alone, adding cadenzas and a coda around a melody built from a three-note phrase.
cues.evidence: Yevgeny Sudbin’s 2005 liner notes identify Beketova’s poem, the 1902 song, the 1913 transcription and its added cadenzas and coda. https://www.yevgenysudbin.com/artist.php?view=prog&rid=458

cues.title: A trill under a fermata
cues.text: The repeated right-hand figures quicken and swell, then stop on a trill under a fermata. The bass holds its chord while the trill fades. A rising flourish releases the pause and the melody continues più mosso, more quickly.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 3, first system: accelerando, crescendo, trill with fermata, diminuendo and più mosso.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The hands share the song
cues.text: On the closing page the melody passes between the hands beneath high, quick notes. A final run marked veloce climbs and falls across the keyboard. The accompaniment keeps turning a little longer, then settles on a quiet A♭ major chord.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 4: melodic hand crossings, veloce run, ritardando and final pp A♭ major chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The trill delays the melody
transitions.from: A · A song inside the triplets
transitions.to: B · A trill holds the music still
transitions.how: The right hand accelerates over a held left-hand chord and reaches a trill, marked f, under a fermata. A diminuendo lets it fade; a rising run leads into più mosso. The left hand keeps its chord through the pause and the melody’s restart.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 3, first system: accelerando, trill with fermata, tied left-hand chord and più mosso.

transitions.title: Four beats, then three again
transitions.from: B · A trill holds the music still
transitions.to: C · High notes and the final run
transitions.how: The quiet a tempo passage reaches a double bar and a single bar of common time. The right hand climbs into the top octave, then the metre returns to 3/4. At mf, the melody crosses between the hands beneath the running semiquavers.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, end of p. 3 and beginning of p. 4: common time, 8va, return to 3/4 and melodic hand crossings.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Solo-piano transcription of the song Lilacs (1902), made by the composer in 1913
fields.note: The RCA register labels the track “Transcription: Rachmaninoff”, DAHR catalogues it as piano solo and Sudbin dates the transcription to summer 1913. The performing edition, and whether the composer varied the printed text, are not identified.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: DAHR’s approved take 9 is dated 27 December 1923; the Archive filename and the RCA register give the same date. Earlier takes from 1920, 1922 and October 1923 were not issued.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: DAHR gives Camden, New Jersey for takes 8–9; the Church Building laboratory is named only for the first take of 1920.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Victor is the original label; the uploader identifies the 1992 RCA/BMG set as the immediate source of the file.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Victor 1051 (10-inch double-faced, coupled with Tchaikovsky’s Humoresque); RCA-BMG 09026 61265 2, CD 10 (1992)
fields.note: Victor 64906 was an earlier single-faced number marked not issued. The disc used for the 1992 transfer is not identified.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: DAHR names the matrix, takes and issues. The link between that take and this digital file rests on the RCA register (which names the matrix and take for the CD track) and the uploader’s CD identification; no waveform or run-out comparison with the disc was made.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: John Pfeiffer, reissue producer; Ward Marston, disc-to-DAT transfer; André Gauthier, remastering supervisor; Anthony Salvatore, remastering engineer
fields.note: These are the credits printed for the 1992 RCA/BMG set. Their connection to this access file rests on the uploader’s identification of the item as CD 10 of that set. The later ripper and uploader are not named as engineers.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The set was issued in 1992, but the dates of the disc-to-DAT transfer, the remastering and the later CD extraction are not stated. The Internet Archive upload of 11 October 2025 is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Disc-to-DAT transfer, then digital remastering at BMG/RCA Studios, New York City; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV.
fields.note: The booklet says surface imperfections were reduced without radical removal of all surface noise. It gives no equalisation, pitch-correction, noise-reduction or editing settings, and none is inferred from the audio analysis.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Rachmaninoff died in 1943. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition. The song text is Ekaterina Beketova’s and the transcription is the composer’s own.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: US public domain: the issued sound recording was published by 1925 (Victor 1051, recorded 1923).
fields.note: DAHR’s catalogue record for Victor 1051 gives a publication date of [1923], and an Internet Archive digitisation of Victrola 1051-A gives 1923; both are catalogue-derived years, not release days. The 1925 Victor catalogue lists “Lilacs (Rachmaninoff, Op. 21, No. 5)” on 1051, which establishes publication no later than 1925 independently of the session date. The Archive item’s Public Domain Mark is noted but not relied on. The 1992 booklet carries an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any new creative contribution to the mastering is cleared worldwide.

composer.epithet: In exile he earned his living at the piano, while the bells of his Russian childhood kept sounding through the music he wrote.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition

Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen, newly graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 sat in the audience applauding. For a young composer, it was an excellent beginning.

His childhood had been less orderly. Born into a landowning family, he grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated; his sister Sofia died of diphtheria; schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the voices and bells that would stay with him. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a move to Moscow, under the formidable care of the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev.
